subject: chemistry
title: Free-radical substitution
key_idea: In ultraviolet light, an alkane reacts with chlorine or bromine by **free-radical substitution**. A halogen atom replaces a hydrogen atom in a chain reaction of **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**. The reaction gives a mixture of products, so it is of limited use in synthesis.

blocks.text: Alkanes are unreactive towards polar reagents. They do react with halogens, but only when radicals are made.

items: The reaction needs **ultraviolet radiation**, which supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond.
It is a **substitution**: one hydrogen atom is replaced by a halogen atom.
Bromine reacts in the same way as chlorine, as in the reaction of ethane with Br₂ to give bromoethane and HBr.
The mechanism involves radicals, formed by homolytic fission.
Alkane + Cl₂ or Br₂, in ultraviolet light, gives a halogenoalkane and a hydrogen halide.
The reaction is a substitution that goes through radicals.

blocks.text: The mechanism has three stages. Each radical is shown with a dot, and the steps are written as equations.

items.meaning: The step that makes radicals from a molecule, by homolytic fission with ultraviolet light.
A step in which a radical reacts with a molecule and makes a new radical, so the chain continues.
A step in which two radicals join to form a molecule, so the chain stops.

rows: Ultraviolet light breaks the Cl–Cl bond homolytically.
A chlorine radical removes H from methane.
The methyl radical makes the product and a new chlorine radical.
Two radicals join to make the product.
Two radicals join to make ethane, a by-product.

diagram.alt: A sequencing task: put the steps of free-radical substitution of methane in order.
diagram.prompt: Put these steps of the chlorination of methane in order.

items: Propagation is a **chain reaction**, because each step makes the radical needed for the next.
One chlorine radical from initiation can lead to thousands of propagation steps.
Every propagation step has one radical on each side. Every termination step has none on the product side.
Dots must go on every radical: Cl•, •CH₃ and •C₂H₅.
Initiation makes radicals, propagation passes them on, termination removes them.
Propagation keeps the chain going: a radical goes in and a radical comes out.

blocks.text: Radical substitution is hard to control. It gives a mixture of products rather than one.

items: **Further substitution**: if there is excess chlorine, CH₃Cl reacts again to give CH₂Cl₂, then CHCl₃ and CCl₄.
**Substitution at different positions**: in a longer chain, the halogen can replace any hydrogen. Propane gives both 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.
The products must be separated, so the yield of the wanted compound is low.
Using a large excess of the alkane makes further substitution less likely.
Radical substitution gives a mixture, from further substitution and from substitution at different carbons.
It is therefore a poor way of making one pure halogenoalkane.

checks.q: Write equations for the initiation and the two propagation steps in the chlorination of methane.
checks.a: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.

checks.q: Write an equation for a termination step that forms ethane, C₂H₆.
Explain why the chlorination of propane is not a good way to make 1-chloropropane.
checks.a: The chlorine radical can replace a hydrogen on any carbon, so 2-chloropropane is also formed. Further substitution can give dichloropropanes, so there is a mixture of products and a low yield of 1-chloropropane.

items: Half curly arrows are not required in this mechanism.
Equations must use a single dot, •, for the unpaired electron on each radical.
Know the reactions of alkanes with oxygen (combustion) and with halogens (radical substitution).
Half curly arrows are not expected in this mechanism.
The example to learn is methane with chlorine.
Explain the reaction as a free-radical substitution with initiation, propagation and termination steps.
Describe the complete and incomplete combustion of alkanes.
Use ethane as the example for the free-radical substitution by Cl₂ or Br₂ in ultraviolet light.
Ethane reacts as CH₃CH₃ + Br₂ → CH₃CH₂Br + HBr, with the same initiation, propagation and termination steps.
